Copper-Catalyzed Enantioselective Radical Cyanation of Allenic
C(sp
2
)−H Bonds to Access Tri- and Tetrasubstituted Chiral Allenes
Daqi Lv, Xiaotao Zhu,* and Hongli Bao*

ABSTRACT: The asymmetric radical functionalization of allenic C(sp
2
)−H bonds represents an appealing strategy for synthesizing
axially chiral allenes. This method enables us to generate the more structurally complex and highly functionalized axially chiral
allenes directly by using the readily accessible and less substituted racemic allenes while concurrently achieving apparent dynamic
kinetic resolution. However, compared to alkyne derivative-based approaches, the asymmetric functionalization of allenic C(sp
2
)−H
bonds remains a challenge primarily due to the intertwined demands of chemo-, regio-, and enantioselectivity. Here, we report a
copper-catalyzed asymmetric cyanation of allenic C(sp
2
)−H bonds by using a substituted oxazoline chiral ligand. This strategy
efficiently transforms low-substituted racemic allenes into highly functionalized, axially chiral allenyl nitriles in a highly chemo-,
regio-, and enantioselective manner.
KEYWORDS: enantioselective cyanation, C−H functionalization, radical, chiral allene, copper catalysis
■
INTRODUCTION
Axially chiral allenes are a class of significant organic molecules,
characterized by their distinctive orthogonal twisted π-
systems.
1
Functionalized allenes often exhibit notable physio-
logical activities, such as enzyme inhibition, cytotoxicity, and
antibacterial properties (Scheme 1a).
2
As a result, structural
modifications of allene compounds or their incorporation into
pharmaceutical molecules to enhance biological activity
represent a key direction for future development in this field.
3
Over the past decade, significant progress has been made in
the development of radical synthesis methods for allenes.
4
Among these advancements, the asymmetric transformation of
allenyl radicals has emerged as a powerful strategy for
constructing axially chiral allenes (Scheme 1b, left). Our
group previously reported the first copper-catalyzed radical 1,4-
bifunctionalization of 1,3-enynes, achieving asymmetric 1,4-
oxycyanation and offering a novel method for synthesizing
elusive axially chiral allenes.
5
Subsequently, Deng et al.
demonstrated a stereoselective decarboxylation strategy for
1,3-enynes using a photoinduced dual catalytic system.
6
Meanwhile, Liu
7
and Guo
8
independently achieved copper-
catalyzed asymmetric 1,4-alkylalkynylation and arylalkynylation
via allenyl radical-terminal alkyne coupling. Notably, He et al.
introduced a nickel-catalyzed radical cascade reaction for
enantio- and regioselective 1,4-arylalkylation of 1,3-enynes.
9
These enantioselective radical 1,4-difunctionalization protocols
collectively provide efficient access to structurally diverse,
enantioenriched tetrasubstituted allenes. Expanding the scope
further, Liu et al. reported copper-catalyzed enantioselective
radical cyanation of propargylic C(sp
3
)−H bonds, delivering
chiral trisubstituted allenyl nitriles.
10
These outstanding works
demonstrate that constructing axially chiral allenes from alkyne
derivatives, such as 1,3-enynes or alkynes, has become a
reliable and promising strategy.
From another perspective, the asymmetric radical function-
alization of allenic C(sp
2
)−H bonds also represents an
attractive strategy for synthesizing axially chiral allenes
(Scheme 1b, right). This approach enables the functionaliza-
tion of readily available low-substituted racemic allenes while
simultaneously achieving apparent dynamic kinetic resolution.
As a result, this provides access to structurally complex and

strategy faces significant challenges, particularly in achieving
satisfactory stereoselective control and the addressing issues of
chemical and regioselectivity during the activation of allenic
C(sp
2
)−H bonds and the transformation of allenyl radicals. In
2016, Lee and colleagues demonstrated the use of peroxyl
radicals to abstract hydrogen atoms from allenic C−H bonds,
thereby generating allenyl radical intermediates.
11
More
recently, Liu
12
and Wu
13
almost simultaneously introduced a
groundbreaking strategy for the functionalization of allenes via
radical activation of allylic C(sp
2
)−H bonds. These elegant
studies achieved high chemoselectivity and regioselectivity,
paving the way for the synthesis of complex and functionalized
allenyl derivatives from simple precursors. Despite these
advances, the asymmetric radical functionalization of allenic
C(sp
2
)−H bonds remains a significant challenge due to the
intertwined demands of chemo- [C(sp
2
)−H vs C(sp
3
)−H
activation vs radical addition], regio- (allenyl vs propargyl
radical pathways), and enantioselectivity (the linear geometry
of allenyl radicals).
12a,13a
In this context, we have conducted extensive studies to
address these challenges, and herein, we report an asymmetric
cyanation reaction of C(sp
2
)−H bonds catalyzed by a copper
complex with a substituted oxazoline (Scheme 1c). This
approach enables the efficient transformation of low-
substituted racemic allenes into highly functionalized, axially
chiral allenyl nitriles under mild conditions. This work not only
addresses the challenges of chemo-, regio-, and enantioselec-
tivity but also highlights the potential of C−H functionaliza-
tion strategies for the synthesis of complex organic molecules.
■
METHODS
Reaction Optimization. To initiate these studies, (1-
methyl-1,2-butadienyl)benzene (1a) was reacted as the model
substrate, with N-fluorobenzenesulfonimide (NFSI) as the
HAT reagent and trimethylsilyl cyanide (2) as the coupling
partner in the presence of a catalytic amount of Cu-

(5 mol %) in acetone at room temperature
for 24 h. To our delight, the desired product 3a was obtained
in 25% yield and 64:36 er when bis(oxazoline) L1 (7.5 mol %)
was used as the ligand (Table 1, entry 1). We then screened a
series of bis(oxazoline) ligands (L2−L7) with different
substituents on R, finding that L7 gave the best result (25%
yield, 91:9 er) (entry 7). At 0 °C, both the yield and er were
improved compared to room temperature (entry 8). Given the
propensity of the reaction substrates to polymerize, a number
of inhibitors were tested as additives.
14
It was found that the
addition of 1 mol % of 4-(trans-4-butylcyclohexyl)phenol (A4)
significantly increased the reaction yield without compromising
the high enantioselectivity. Finally, examination of different
copper salts showed that CuBr
2
was the best choice, yielding
58% yield, 93:7 er (for details of optimization of the
conditions, see Supporting Information). Therefore, the
optimal conditions were established as CuBr
2

Substrate Scope. Having established the optimized
reaction conditions, we tested a variety of substituted allenes
to probe the versatility of our catalytic system (Scheme 2). A
variety of enantioenriched tetrasubstituted allenyl nitriles (3a−
3y) were obtained in moderate to good yields (43−62%) and
with high enantiomeric ratios (82:18−97:3 er). Allene
substrates with electron-donating or electron-withdrawing
groups introduced at various positions on the aromatic ring
can provide the corresponding products (3a−3h) with an er
value as high as 97:3. Moreover, other aromatic rings such as
the naphthyl group (3i and 3j) and thienyl group (3k) are
tolerated. A screening of the R
1
and R
2
revealed that alkyl
chains (3l−3q), phosphonate group (3r), silyl ether group
(3s), chloroalkyl group (3t), benzyl group (3u), and vinyl
groups (3v and 3w) are tolerated. Notably, a diverse array of
substrates, encompassing those with benzyl C−H bonds (3u)
as well as allyl C−H bonds (3v and 3w), have been selectively
transformed through the cyanation of the allenic C(sp
2
)−H
bond, affording the target products without the observation of
C(sp
3
)−H bond cyanation. The absolute configuration of
axially chiral allenyl nitriles 3c was unambiguously confirmed
by X-ray analysis. Both 3x
12a
and 3y
13a
can also be obtained in
good yields as well as with higher enantioselectivities by our
method. To showcase the practical application of our method,
the allenic C(sp
2
)−H cyanation reaction was scaled up to a 10
mmol batch. This amplification synthesis exhibits even higher
enantioselectivity compared to standard conditions (3a, 96:4
er and 3y, 93:7 er), highlighting the enormous synthetic
potential of our method.
The versatility of this strategy extends to the synthesis of
trisubstituted allenyl nitriles. Under the standard reaction
conditions, a spectrum of enantioenriched trisubstituted allenyl
nitriles (5a−5j) was successfully synthesized. The process
demonstrates the well tolerance for diverse functional groups,
including phenyl (5a−5c), naphthyl (5d), benzothiophene
(5e), and secondary and tertiary alkyl groups (5f and 5g).
Products 5h−5j can also be obtained in good yields as well as
with higher enantioselectivities by our method.
12a,13a
More-
over, scaling up the reaction has led to a further enhancement
in enantioselectivity, as evidenced by product 5c, which
achieved an enantiomeric ratio of 96:4.
Further Transformations. Such obtained enantioenriched
allenyl nitriles potentially have wide applications in organic
synthesis (Scheme 3). For example, the reduction of allenyl
nitrile 3a with 1.1 equiv of DIBAL-H efficiently yields allenyl
aldehyde 6,
15
which can be further reduced to produce allenyl
propanol 7. Additionally, chiral allenyl nitrile 3a can be readily
transformed into allenyl amide 8 in a high yield through
hydrolysis. In the presence of potassium hydroxide, compound
3a can be fully hydrolyzed to generate the corresponding acid
9.
15

mechanism, we conducted a series of experiments (Scheme
4a−f). Initial radical scavenger studies using 2,2,6,6-tetrame-

standard conditions completely suppressed product formation,

confirming a radical-mediated pathway (Scheme 4a). A radical-
clock experiment with an alkenyl cyclopropane substrate
generated the ring-opening product (15), directly evidencing
the allenyl radical intermediate (Scheme 4b). Kinetic isotope
effect studies (k
H
/k
D
= 2.3) suggest that intermolecular
hydrogen atom abstraction might be the rate-limiting step
(Scheme 4c).
We then proceeded to investigate the nonlinear effects in
this method and found that allenyl nitrile 3a indeed exhibited
linear effects (Scheme 4d).
18
This led us to consider that a
monoligand copper complex acts as the active catalytic species
in the reaction.
19
To delve deeper into the structure of the
metal complex, we conducted control experiments under
standard conditions using ligand L8, with its hydroxyl group
protected by trimethylsilyl; these results closely mirrored those
obtained under standard conditions (Scheme 4e, 58% yield,
93:7 er vs 50% yield, 93:7 er). This finding implies that the
hydroxyl group as an electron-donating group may be a
spectator and the hydrogen bonding may not play a role in the
metal complex. Furthermore, the structure of L7CuBr
2
(16)
was elucidated through X-ray crystallography, revealing the
complex composed of a single copper atom and a single ligand
(Scheme 4f). Upon subjecting this crystal to a cyanation
reaction as the catalyst, we observed that the reaction
efficiencies and enantioselectivities were nearly identical to
those under standard conditions (47% yield, 92:8 er), thereby
validating the existence of a monoligand copper active species.
This is also consistent with the conclusions drawn from the
linear effect observed earlier.
Drawing from these experimental outcomes, we propose a
potential catalytic cycle mechanism (Scheme 5). Initially, a
monovalent monoligand copper species A undergoes single-
electron transfer with NFSI, leading to the formation of a
divalent fluorinated copper species B and a nitrogen radical.
This nitrogen radical can abstract the C(sp
2
)−H bond from
the allene, forming an allenyl radical.
12a,13a
The divalent
fluorinated copper species B then undergoes transmetalation
with TMSCN, yielding cyanated copper intermediate C.
Ultimately, intermediate C engages in an asymmetric func-
tional group transfer with the allenyl radical, yielding the target
product and regenerating the catalyst.
20
■
CONCLUSIONS
In conclusion, we have developed a copper-catalyzed
enantioselective radical cyanation of allenic C(sp
2
)−H bonds
under mild reaction conditions, enabling efficient access to
trisubstituted and tetrasubstituted axially chiral allenyl nitriles.
This strategy achieves high chemoselectivity, regioselectivity,
and enantioselectivity, with broad functional group tolerance.
Mechanistic studies corroborate a radical pathway involving a
monoligand copper species. The synthetic utility of this
method is further highlighted by its scalability (10 mmol scale)
and the versatile downstream derivatization with a chiral
quaternary carbon center of chiral allenyl nitriles into cyclic
ether, lactam, and butenolides. We believe that this work may
open up new possibilities of allenic C(sp
2
)−H asymmetric
functionalization, offering a promising entry to highly
functionalized axially chiral allene derivatives.

ABSTRACT: The asymmetric radical functionalization of allenic C(sp<sup>2</sup>)−H bonds represents an appealing strategy for synthesizing
axially chiral allenes. This method enables us to generate the more structurally complex and highly functionalized axially chiral
allenes directly by using the readily accessible and less substituted racemic allenes while concurrently achieving apparent dynamic
kinetic resolution. However, compared to alkyne derivative-based approaches, the asymmetric functionalization of allenic C(sp<sup>2</sup>)−H
bonds remains a challenge primarily due to the intertwined demands of chemo-, regio-, and enantioselectivity. Here, we report a
copper-catalyzed asymmetric cyanation of allenic
\mathrm { C } ( \mathsf { s p } ^ { 2 } ) \mathrm { - H }
bonds by using a substituted oxazoline chiral ligand. This strategy
eficiently transforms low-substituted racemic allenes into highly functionalized, axially chiral allenyl nitriles in a highly chemo-,
regio-, and enantioselective manner.
KEYWORDS: enantioselective cyanation, C−H functionalization, radical, chiral allene, copper catalysis
■ INTRODUCTION

Axially chiral allenes are a class of significant organic molecules,
characterized by their distinctive orthogonal twisted π-
systems.<sup>1</sup> Functionalized allenes often exhibit notable physio-
logical activities, such as enzyme inhibition, cytotoxicity, and
antibacterial properties (Scheme 1a).<sup>2</sup> As a result, structural
modifications of allene compounds or their incorporation into
pharmaceutical molecules to enhance biological activity
represent a key direction for future development in this field.<sup>3</sup>

Drawing from these experimental outcomes, we propose a
potential catalytic cycle mechanism (Scheme 5). Initially, a
monovalent monoligand copper species A undergoes single-
electron transfer with NFSI, leading to the formation of a

divalent fluorinated copper species B and a nitrogen radical.
This nitrogen radical can abstract the
\mathbf { C } ( \mathbf { s p } ^ { 2 } ) \mathrm { - H }

fluorinated copper species B then undergoes transmetalation
with TMSCN, yielding cyanated copper intermediate C.
Ultimately, intermediate C engages in an asymmetric func-
tional group transfer with the allenyl radical, yielding the target
product and regenerating the catalyst.
■ CONCLUSIONS

In conclusion, we have developed a copper-catalyzed
enantioselective radical cyanation of allenic
\mathrm { C } ( \mathsf { s p } ^ { 2 } ) \mathrm { - H }
bonds
under mild reaction conditions, enabling eficient access to
trisubstituted and tetrasubstituted axially chiral allenyl nitriles.
This strategy achieves high chemoselectivity, regioselectivity,
and enantioselectivity, with broad functional group tolerance.
Mechanistic studies corroborate a radical pathway involving a
monoligand copper species. The synthetic utility of this
method is further highlighted by its scalability (10 mmol scale)
and the versatile downstream derivatization with a chiral
quaternary carbon center of chiral allenyl nitriles into cyclic
ether, lactam, and butenolides. We believe that this work may
open up new possibilities of allenic C(sp<sup>2</sup>)−H asymmetric
functionalization, ofering a promising entry to highly
functionalized axially chiral allene derivatives.
